## Full 1977-2014 detail cut from the main narrative {#detail-1977-2014}

**The three subperiods** (grounded in the digitized UCLA General Catalogs 2003–05 through
2013–14, per `evidence/deep-research-report.md`; Sears's dates independently confirmed):
- **ISSR proper, 1977 – late 2000s.** An OECD international directory dates the "ISSR Data Archive
  at UCLA" to December 1977, for quantitative research "primarily secondary analysis," drawing on
  UCLA's ICPSR membership plus federal statistical agencies (Census, NCHS, NCES, BLS) and local
  studies like LACSS.
- **Institute for Social Research (ISR), ~2009–2011.** Parent institute renamed by the 2009–10
  UCLA General Catalog, same phone, same components including the Data Archive, new website
  (`isr.ucla.edu`). Still in the 2010–11 catalog. No director identified under this name.
- **Standalone SSDA, ~2011–2014.** By the 2011–12 catalog neither ISSR nor ISR appears; SSDA is
  listed independently as a Social Sciences collection with its own site (`dataarchives.ss.ucla.edu`).
  No public source names a formal dissolution of the parent or a single successor. The reporting
  line from here to the 2014 Library transfer is unresolved.
- Immediately pre-transfer (2013), SSDA was piloting the DDI-Lifecycle metadata standard and
  Colectica curation software.
- **Southern California Social Survey (SCSS)**, confirmed running 1984-1991 in the Harvard
  Dataverse SSDA collection (true start year not pinned down, likely closer to 1977-1980, never
  deposited in ICPSR at all).
- 1988 technical infrastructure detail: mainframe (IBM 3090, MVS/VM-CMS), tape management
  (DTA/DTB numbering system), UCLA's ORION catalog, ICPSR's SPIRES search facility, a
  microcomputer-based (dBase III) tape-tracking system Pawlocki and Stephenson built
  [@pawlockiStephenson1988].
- Rotating annual LACSS PIs: Lawrence Bobo (1992, then UCLA Assoc. Professor of Sociology).
- Cross-national work in more depth: the Intergenerational Stratification and Mobility File
  (ISMF), built with Harry Ganzeboom (Free University, Amsterdam) and Donald Treiman, funded by
  the Netherlands Organisation for Scientific Research (NWO), Project H50.293
  [@stilesStephenson2008].

See `evidence/pawlocki-stephenson-1988-iassist.md`, `evidence/lamas-scss-lacss-series.md`,
`evidence/stiles-stephenson-2008-ifla.md`.

## Norman Powell's gifts, full detail {#powell-gifts}

Per UCLA Library's own retrospective, at least five distinct gifts, only one precisely dated:

1. December 15, 2016, $5 million, endowed the University Librarian position itself (named the
   "Norman and Armena Powell University Librarian"). Confirmed via UCLA Newsroom press release.
2. A data scientist position, funded as part of early support for UCLA's Sustainable LA Grand
   Challenge, undated in every source checked.
3. A deep learning machine and Data Science Center space enhancements in the Charles E. Young
   Research Library, undated.
4. DataSquad seed funding, undated. (DataSquad itself: "Founder and Lead, UCLA DataSquad
   student consulting program, 2021 – present," per Tim's Data Summary, so the seed funding
   predates or coincides with 2021, narrowing the undated range somewhat.)
5. Support for the Library's acquisition of the Barbara and Willard Morgan Photographs and
   Papers, matching other donors' gifts toward the same acquisition, undated.

## Full visualization methodology {#chart-methods}

**Survey-year bar chart** (titled "Survey years represented in the surviving SSDA collection"
since 2026-09-27; earlier drafts called it "holdings activity," which overstated what it shows):
571 datasets in the Harvard Dataverse SSDA collection
(`dataverse.harvard.edu/dataverse/ssda_ucla`), pulled via the collection's search API 2026-08-09,
bucketed by the survey year embedded in each dataset's title (regex-matched, last 4-digit year
1930-2026 in the title string), not the Dataverse "published" date (uniformly 2015-2018, a
migration artifact). This is a distinct, smaller number from the "1,014 legacy Social Science
Data Archive datasets" Tim's own Data Summary says were harvested into UCLA's own live Dataverse
instance, different scope (Harvard-hosted historical sub-collection vs. UCLA's current live
instance), don't conflate the two counts.

**Citation event plot**: queried live via browser automation against ICPSR's per-study
"Data-related Publications" search (`icpsr.umich.edu/sites/icpsr/search/publications?q=STUDY_NO:{n}`),
2026-08-09, this endpoint is Cloudflare-blocked to scripted/curl access (confirmed, HTTP 403),
which is why browser automation was needed. Checked: all 5 confirmed LACSS study records
(36599, 36600, 36598, 36563, 36749) and all 8 confirmed LAMAS waves (36631, 36612, 36611, 36624,
36615, 36614, 36607, 36617). SCSS was searched separately for its own ICPSR presence and found
to have none, it was never deposited there, confirmed via a direct ICPSR search for "Southern
California Social Survey" (only the 5 LACSS records matched, as background-text mentions, not
actual SCSS deposits).

See `evidence/icpsr-citation-count-lamas-lacss.md` and `evidence/lamas-scss-lacss-series.md`.

## Full 2018–present account {#dsc-era-detail}

The longer version of the 2018–present chapter, moved here from the main history on 2026-09-27
when that chapter was reorganized around four cases. It is kept intact (apart from corrected
3D-scan credit and editorial notes moved to [Open questions](#open-questions)), so it overlaps
the main text in places. Hosted collections, the Daniels inventory, and the Powell gifts have
their own sections below.

This is the era with the widest gap between the unit's size and its reach, and the era this
history's author directed. It is written against institutional records and cited sources rather
than recollection, and the judgments in it are marked as judgments. Working notes and the full
evidence trail are in `evidence/library-era-2014-present.md` and
this companion.

### Continuity, not rupture

The 2018 rebrand changed the unit's name and widened its scope. It did not replace what came
before. `ucla-data-archive_old`, a repository built around the "Data Archive" identity, holding
its collections policies, terms, and deposit and preservation practices, was created in July
2017 and actively maintained through May 2020, two years after the unit's formal name became
"Data Science Center." The archive's core work, repository hosting, which descends directly from
the LAMAS, SCSS, and LACSS series, ran under the new name the whole time. Jina "Jamie" Jamison,
who came across with the archive in 2014, still leads that repository work today. She is the one
human through-line across the whole Library era.

The growth over that span is easy to state. Staff went from 2.0 FTE at the 2014 transfer (a
director and a data archivist) to five by about 2021, mostly by redesigning existing library
positions rather than hiring new ones: a geospatial librarian moved in from another department
and was rebuilt as a Spatial Data Science Librarian (Zhiyuan Yao), a data manager from the
Library's IT division was rebuilt as a Data Science Facilitator, and a Digital Library programmer
with a machine-learning background was recruited across divisions (Kristian Allen, a 0.5-FTE
role, 2018–2024).[^c-staff-model] UCLA Dataverse went from 9 datasets and 229 downloads in January
2020 to roughly 1,600 datasets and more than 143,000 downloads by 2026.[^c-dataverse-count] The
staffing did not grow in proportion. Part of how the unit absorbed the load is the student
program described below; part is that some capacity was simply lost, a GIS position cut in 2024
and other roles ended, with the demand in those areas still there.

[^c-staff-model]: Dennis et al. 2021 [@dennisEtal2021] describes the redesign-not-hire staffing
model. The specific position histories rest partly on the author's account.

[^c-dataverse-count]: The "~1,600" resolves an apparent discrepancy. UCLA Dataverse holds about
376 datasets deposited directly at UCLA plus about 1,014 legacy Social Science Data Archive
datasets harvested in and curated by Library staff, which is roughly 1,390 released, or 1,603
counting drafts and restricted deposits. The research site's figure for the directly deposited slice was about 377 in August 2026 and
about 395 in September 2026. See `evidence/library-era-2014-present.md` §4.

### What stayed constant, and what changed

For six decades and five institutional homes the constant has been the same: keep research
evidence findable, usable, and preserved, and extend that to whatever kind of evidence
researchers happened to be producing. What changed after 2018 is the range of things that
covers. Not only survey datasets now, but restricted and sensitive data that needs governed
computation, geospatial data and aerial imagery, 3D and spatial capture, text corpora and
computational text analysis, research software, and course material treated as a citable
output.[^c-text] Look back at that list and it tracks the field's own sequence, from data citation
to open and FAIR data to open science to software curation to computationally intensive research
support. That is a way of narrating what changed after the fact, not a plan anyone was working
to. The sections below take the main strands one at a time.

[^c-text]: The text strand shows up two ways. As teaching, DSC ran a well-attended line of
workshops on qualitative and text data ("What do I do with all of this text? Cleaning and coding
data for qualitative analysis," "Getting started with qualitative data analysis"), visible in
the in-progress DSC instruction-stats integration. As consulting, the DSC team's 2021 chapter
[@dennisEtal2021] gives a worked example, helping a graduate student analyze ancient Buddhist
texts with natural-language-processing techniques. The OCR and machine-learning work that grew
out of it is under "Text, OCR, and machine learning" below.

### The repository: UCLA Dataverse

The legacy SSDA collection had lived on Harvard's hosted Dataverse. In 2018 the DSC stood up a
local UCLA instance, chosen for the same reasons the archive had chosen Dataverse in the first
place: DDI metadata, the ability to restrict licensed data, and a curation ladder from
self-service deposit to fully mediated. The DSC wired it to UCLA single sign-on, DOI minting,
and preservation through the California Digital Library. Research groups run their own branded
sub-collections inside it with DSC training, and the Library uses it to manage discovery and
access for data it buys.[@dennisEtal2021] One deliberate choice was to harvest the legacy SSDA
collection into the discovery layer rather than migrate it right away: keep it working first,
move it later.

Growth came in three steps. Late 2021 was the institutional scale-up, when schools and centers
began running their own collections. Mid to late 2022 brought the legacy SSDA holdings into the
local discovery layer, along with wider campus adoption. From 2023 on the growth was steady. By
January 2026 the repository had 135 collections (92 published), 312 user accounts, and about
54,700 released files. The day-to-day work was Jamie Jamison's. She wrote the preservation
documentation, represented UCLA at the 2021 Dataverse Community Meeting, and kept the
continuity guarantees working: automated nightly database dumps to cloud storage, consolidated
storage buckets, current certificates, and a tested scripted install so the system could be
rebuilt if it had to be. She walked depositors through sub-collections, DOIs, and archiving,
handled access to the LARIAC imagery, and when Redivis arrived became the first approver for
restricted-data requests. She is named as data manager on the published L2 voter dataset.

The collections DSC hosts now run well past social science. The UCLA Law Behind Bars Data
Project covers COVID-19 in prisons, jails, and detention nationally, about 1,169 items. The
Williams Institute's LGBT law-and-policy data, which DSC curation helped bring to ICPSR
directly, includes TransPop, the first national probability sample of transgender people in the
US. The Cotsen Institute and DIG archaeology collections hold about 6,360 items in DIG alone,
more than the whole historical SSDA, LAMAS, SCSS, and LACSS corpus put together. DIG's own stated
aim, to "expand citation practices" in archaeology, is the same bibliographic-control instinct
Stephenson brought to the 1980s, applied to a different field at a much larger scale.

Reuse is harder to count than deposits. Of about 959 indexed datasets, 180 carry a link to a
publication, and 13 of those papers can be traced in OpenAlex, with 258 citations between them.
That is a floor, not an estimate. A DataCite export bug drops links, restricted and draft
datasets are left out, archaeology datasets tied to books have no DOI to follow, and about 200
public datasets have no publication link on file. The traceable depositors include a
radiation-belt modeling group in Earth, Planetary, and Space Sciences led by Yuri Shprits that
deposits again and again (four linked papers, 95 citations).

Running a repository also meant defending it. In early 2025, bots mass-downloaded UCLA Dataverse
content, apparently to train a model, rotating across thousands of addresses to get around IP
blocking, from about April to July. Tim identified an open-source bot filter, Anubis, as the fix,
and Jamison put it into production and tuned it, with host-level blocking alongside, so that
abusive traffic was stopped without locking out researchers. The attack was contained by
summer with no loss to the collection.[^c-bots]

[^c-bots]: Tim Dennis, Statement of Professional Achievements, 2023–2025, and DSC internal
records for 2025–26.

### Consulting: from reference desk to research partner

The archive had always answered questions: data discovery, codebook lookups, help with SPSS,
SAS, and Stata. The 2018 redesign kept that and widened it. The DSC's new mission statement,
written through a design-thinking exercise that put the scholar at the center, named the whole
research life cycle: planning and data management plans, acquisition, storage, cleaning,
analysis, publication, curation, and preservation.[@dennisEtal2021] In practice that meant
consultations on data cleaning, visualization, coding, and methods such as text and cluster
analysis. As the team's skills grew it added GIS, 3D and drone capture, machine learning,
research software, reproducible workflows, and open-source licensing.

Not all of it happened one-on-one. The team ran Tidy Tuesday, a weekly social data-cleaning
lab; judged an inaugural datathon with an Anderson student group in spring 2020; and helped
program a UC-wide Love Data Week of more than 25 workshops and events. It taught inside degree
programs too: the Sustainable LA Grand Challenge undergraduate scholars, the Mellon Mays fellows,
and graduate programs in social science, urban planning, applied statistics, and
management.[@dennisEtal2021]

The volume is documented for the later years. From 2023 to 2025 the unit logged at least 1,175
service interactions: 785 scheduled consultations, 156 service-desk tickets, and 234 tracked
project collaborations. The School of Public Affairs, the Social Sciences division, and Life
Sciences brought the most consultations. Over the same years the work changed shape, from single
appointments toward project support that ran for months, and the longest of those engagements
are in [Research impact](history.html#evidence-of-use).[^c-consults]

[^c-consults]: Counts from LibInsight, Jira, and Trello exports compiled for a 2025–26 review; the
total is conservative, since not every interaction was logged. Other audits give 604 and 741
direct consultations for different windows, and these are not yet reconciled.

### Governed computation: Redivis and the L2 voter file

Before this, UCLA had no campus service for restricted data of this class outside Mednet, the
medical enterprise's computing environment (with HIPAA-level services such as a HIPAA-compliant
Box), which the rest of campus could not use. There was no governed way to give a student access
to a voter file, and no secure place outside medicine to merge FERPA-, PII-, or PHI-restricted
data at scale (author's account, 2026-09-27). To support that class of
data, DSC selected and licensed Redivis, ran the institutional compliance review (Third-Party
Risk Management, P3/P4 approval), negotiated access to the restricted datasets, piloted the
platform in 2022, and launched the governed service in January 2023. It set up a 50-seat model
with data-use-agreement controls so that routine requests would not pile up on one person.[^c-redivis-source]

The main case is the L2 historic voter file, more than 10 TB of national voter history bought
through the archive's gift fund. It arrived as thousands of fragmented state-level files, too
large to store locally and too inconsistent to analyze. DSC pulled it into a single
version-controlled national dataset, published with its own DOI (UCLA Library, *L2 Voter History
and Demographic Dataset*, 2023, doi:10.60603/D37P4R) and presented at FORCE11 2024 by Redivis's
CEO alongside the doctoral student who curated it, Graham Straus. Straus put the institutional
point plainly: "What happens when I leave UCLA? Will people know how the dataset was constructed?
Yes!" Researchers use it directly across departments, in election administration, gentrification,
Latino voting, and a project merging the voter file with UCLA medical records to study health
and voting. Recorded processing on the platform grew from 444 GB in its first year to 2.9 PB in
2024; those figures measure platform activity, not data held (holdings are about 20 TB). DSC
provided the environment and the access. The scholarship stayed with the researchers. The point
of it is not an "AI" story. It is that stewardship came to include governed computation, not
only acquiring and describing open files.

[^c-redivis-source]: Platform and governance detail: Tim Dennis, Statement of Professional
Achievements and Data Summary, 2023–2025, self-reported. The DOI, the FORCE11 presentation
(Mathews & Straus 2024, doi:10.5281/zenodo.13181256), and the publication venues are the
independently checkable parts. Launch: piloted 2022, governed service launched January 2023
(confirmed by Tim 2026-09-02; reconciles the July-2022 / January-2023 sources).

### Infrastructure: running it in the cloud

Almost none of this ran on hardware DSC owned. UCLA Dataverse runs on Amazon Web Services, with
its files in S3, about 5.4 TiB counting replication as of May 2025. The point-cloud service
described below runs on its own AWS server with about 4.5 TiB of storage, shared with the LARIAC
imagery. Redivis is a licensed platform, not a local system. The exceptions were a
deep-learning workstation in the Young Research Library, bought with a Powell gift; the 3D
workstation and drone kit; and an R server DSC hosted for research groups whose data outgrew
their own machines, Carceral Ecologies among them.

Paying for it took a sequence of moves. Dataverse first ran under an AWS account belonging to
the Library's IT division. When campus consolidated its AWS accounts, the cost landed on DSC.
Powell infrastructure funds covered it until they ran out, and then the archive's own gift fund
took over. That last step depended on a budget change made earlier. DSC moved the archive's
large recurring subscriptions, ICPSR and Roper, off its own gift fund and onto the Library's
general membership budget, the way research libraries usually treat major database
memberships. That freed the archive's original fund to cover the cloud costs of Dataverse and
the point-cloud platform. The move was possible because one role could see the archive's budget
and the infrastructure budget at the same time.[^c-funding]

Keeping the systems current was its own work. By 2025 production ran Dataverse 5.14, a release
line upstream no longer patches, and DSC had begun rebuilding the service as code: Terraform for
the AWS resources, an Ansible playbook forked from the Dataverse community's, and a managed
Postgres database, with the 6.x series as the target. That rebuild was not finished where this
history stops.

[^c-funding]: The direction of the subscription move and the reinvestment into infrastructure is
confirmed by budget ledgers and AWS cost records; the full dollar trail, and the dates two other
subscriptions were dropped, is only partly reconstructed. See `evidence/library-era-2014-present.md`
§13.

### Teaching: The Carpentries and an instructor network

Instruction went through three distinct eras, and the shift between them was reactive, not
planned. With two staff and tens of thousands of potential learners, the unit joined The
Carpentries in 2017 and used the membership to build an instructor community rather than hire
one; Tim founded UCLA Carpentries in 2018 and spent its first two years teaching locally, one
campus, in person. Between October 2017 and January 2020 the program ran six Software and Data
Carpentry workshops on campus, in R and Python, at the Young Research Library, Powell Library,
the IDRE Portal, the Mathematical Sciences building, and the LA Kretz Garden Pavilion for
Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, alongside Library Carpentry workshops for librarians and
information-studies students in 2017, 2018, and 2019. The instructor rosters show the model
working: by the two January 2020 workshops, campus volunteers trained through the program were
leading the teaching and DSC staff were mostly helping. COVID changed the economics of that model overnight: travel-based cross-campus
training became impossible, but virtual delivery made cross-campus *coordination* suddenly
cheap. Tim co-founded the systemwide UC Carpentries network in 2020 in direct response to that
constraint, not as a planned expansion, with Berkeley, San Diego, Santa Barbara, Merced, and
Riverside as partner campuses. What followed was sustained, not temporary: nine workshops in
September 2024 alone drew 937 attendances across UCLA and partner UC campuses, and the 2025
series drew 558 attendees (139 from UCLA) across another nine sessions. The unit had gone from
teaching its own campus to running system-scale infrastructure other campuses scheduled their
own programming around, a change in kind, not just volume.

The Carpentries model mattered as much for who taught as for what was taught. The DSC adopted a
Code of Conduct adapted from the Carpentries' own. Every member of the DSC team trained as a
Carpentries instructor, and by 2021 the program had added 13 active instructors, six of them
from technical roles elsewhere in the Library: programmers, a digital asset coordinator, a
technical product owner. Jamison became a regular lead instructor for the Unix shell in the
UC-wide series and wrote a new lesson on Rclone for moving research data. Teaching gave those staff a reason to share what they knew, and gave
DSC instructors it could never have hired. Library Carpentry lessons taught librarians and
library-school students the same data and coding skills, which made the Library's public-facing
staff better partners on data-heavy research.[@dennisEtal2021]

What was taught followed demand. GIS was the largest single category every year, and Geography
the largest single departmental audience. Qualitative and text-data analysis was a steady line,
as were data management plans for the NIH data-sharing policy, high-performance computing,
visualization, and 3D data. Machine learning and AI grew from a handful of sessions in 2023.

Tim's own Carpentries work went past UCLA. An Instructor Trainer since 2016, he received the
Carpentries' Community Service Award in 2018, served on the inaugural Trainers Leadership
Committee and co-wrote its bylaws, and edited a full revision of the Instructor Training
curriculum. As chair of Library Carpentry's Curriculum Advisory Committee from 2022 he moved six
lessons into the official worldwide curriculum, among them DMP 101, a data management plans
lesson aligned to the NIH data-sharing policy. He later co-chaired the Library Carpentry
Governance Group, which sets lesson-adoption standards for the global program.

### Open science and software curation

The IMLS grant RE-252335-OLS-22 ($237,839, Tim as Project Director) [@imls-re252335] treated
course material itself as a citable research output: 15 peer-reviewed open-science lessons
against 14 proposed, each with a Zenodo DOI, CRediT contributor roles, ORCID identifiers, and
Citation File Format metadata, built by 27 authors across 14 teams. Todd Grappone was Co-PI and
Zhiyuan Yao, DSC's spatial data science librarian, coordinated the program; Tim wrote the
computational thinking and R lessons and rewrote the Python one. It is the clearest case of the
software-curation and open-science strands in this era, and, because a federal award can be
checked without anyone's account of it, the one with the firmest outside evidence.

Tim is also Co-PI on the $1.85M Sloan Foundation grant that established the UC OSPO Network, a
six-campus effort to treat open-source software as real scholarly infrastructure. That grant
funds the network, not DSC. What DSC got out of it is a local UCLA open-source program office,
the lead on the network's education work, and shared services (licensing guidance, a repository
browser, a summer student research program). The need is concrete: a 2025 scan of about 81,000
UC-affiliated code repositories found that 77.5% carried no license at all.

The open-science work also ran through the field's own organizations. Tim has been a Center for
Open Science ambassador since 2016 and taught in the Berkeley Initiative for Transparency in the
Social Sciences' Research Transparency and Reproducibility Training, and the Library held a
Center for Open Science institutional membership in 2019–20. DSC staff maintain or co-maintain
Carpentries lessons taught worldwide, from the Unix shell and R to newer lessons on qualitative
data, Wikidata, and using AI coding agents in research without giving up validation and
reproducibility.

### Spatial data and GIS

Geography has consistently been the unit's largest single workshop audience. Before the GIS
position was cut in 2024, DSC's geospatial librarian handled 70 to 80 booked consultations a
year, started the systemwide UC GIS Week, ran UC GIS workshops that reached hundreds of people,
managed the LARIAC regional aerial-imagery holdings (bought through the archive's gift fund),
and worked with UC San Diego and UC Santa Barbara on geospatial discovery for Dataverse. DSC
also ran UCLA's campus ArcGIS Online platform. It grew to more than 7,000 accounts and over
3,000 active users a year, and since the position was cut it has run past its licensed storage
with no assigned administrator.[^c-gis]

[^c-gis]: GIS consultation counts and the ArcGIS figures: DSC statistics and Tim Dennis's Data
Summary, 2023–2025, cross-checked against an OARC governance report (Dec 2025) for the account
totals.

### Emerging technology: 3D capture, drones, and Potree

When the DSC planned its growth in 2018, it named three areas to build toward as it added
staff: GIS, augmented and virtual reality, and machine learning.[@dennisEtal2021] The second
came through Doug Daniels, whose own career crosses the 2018 line. He joined the Library in 2013
on the help desk, built its first 3D printing service as a technical projects specialist, and
from 2016 ran the Lux Lab, the Library's emerging-technology space for 3D printing and scanning,
laser cutting, large-format printing, and VR. In April 2020, after finishing his MLIS, he joined
DSC as Emerging Technologies Librarian.[@ucla-library-doug-daniels-bio] His first months in the
role were the pandemic's, and the lab's printers went to producing protective equipment.

The capture work came first. Daniels scanned objects for partners across campus and beyond:
Egyptian artifacts at the Getty and the Museo Egizio in Turin with the Cotsen Institute (2018),
cuneiform tablets in Library Special Collections, Fowler Museum objects, sarcophagus lids at
LACMA, and Scripps's research vessel FLIP (2021). Medicine became a steady partner: cadaver-arm
scans across dissection stages with the Anatomy Lab (2022), now taught in History of Medicine;
eye tissue scanned for machine-learning measurement at the Stein Eye Institute; thyroid
specimens for Endocrinology (2025); and a 3D-printed surgical probe holder, built with an
undergraduate, now in clinical use at Ronald Reagan UCLA Medical Center. The Easter Island Moai
scans with Jo Anne Van Tilburg (2022) became a chapter in the Cotsen Institute's illustrated
atlas of the statues.

In 2023 DSC added a field kit: a drone with LiDAR and photogrammetry payloads, an RTK base
station for survey-grade positioning, and a dedicated 3D workstation, flown by Daniels under an
FAA remote-pilot certificate. It went to Iceland's Mosfell Valley with a Cotsen doctoral
student for a valley-scale survey (one trip, 2024, per Tim 2026-09-02; the Research Enabled by DSC claim
register does not yet approve a year, see Open questions), and to ongoing temple mapping at Angkor. It also went, twice,
to Powell Library: a terrestrial LiDAR scan in 2021 and a drone survey in 2024, of the building
named for the family whose gifts funded much of DSC's growth.

Capture raised the archive's oldest question in a new form: once the object is recorded, how
does anyone else use it? A point cloud from a survey is usually too large to open as a single
file in a browser or to hand out from a download page. DSC's answer was pointcloud.ucla.edu, a
service built on the open-source Potree viewer, which streams large point clouds so they can be
explored interactively on the web. Lighter models went to the Lux Lab's Sketchfab collection.
The work stayed tied to standards. Daniels chairs the UC 3D Data Common Knowledge Group (a
member from 2020, chair from 2024), which built the ALA-funded 3D Atlas; co-chairs the
international IIIF 3D Community Group; and belongs to the IMLS-funded Community Standards for
3D Preservation effort.

Students carried a share of it. The Lux Lab had its own student line until 2024, when its
funding became restricted and it merged into DataSquad. The best-known result is the Refugee
Material Culture Initiative: with Professor Kelly Nguyen and the Vietnamese Heritage Museum,
Daniels 3D scanned the "Boat of Hope," a river sampan that carried nine refugees out of Vietnam
in 1984, and prepared the models for the museum's public seven-day narrative of one family's
escape; DataSquad student Bianca Badajos helped set up the Potree viewer that hosts it (credit per
the Research Enabled by DSC claim register, 2026-09-27).
Daniels was named a UCLA Librarian of the Year for 2026, one of two given university-wide by
LAUC-LA.[@ucla-newsroom-librarians-2026] His work also ran back to the donor relationship: he
showed the lab to the Powell Society donor circle at open houses in 2017, 2018, and 2019.

### Text, OCR, and machine learning

Machine learning was one of the three areas the DSC planned to grow into in 2018, and it arrived
the way most of the unit's capacity did, through people rather than a new department. Kristian
Allen, a Digital Library programmer with a machine-learning background, joined at half time in
2018. Leigh Phan, on the team from 2017, started as a programmer; her early traces in the record
are web maps for the archive's site in 2018. In 2021 her job was rewritten around computational
research, with machine learning and AI as its main line, and she became the DSC's data
scientist. A Powell gift paid for a deep-learning workstation in the Young Research Library, the
unit's first local GPU capacity. Phan ran it, loaded it with open-source models researchers
could use locally, and when water damage ended the first machine, led the choice of its
replacement.[^c-ml-people]

Text came first as teaching. A line of workshops on qualitative and text data, on cleaning and
coding text for qualitative analysis and on open tools for qualitative methods, drew steadily
from 2021 on. In consulting it showed up as individual projects: comparing Ming dynasty Buddhist
texts with natural-language-processing methods for a graduate student in Asian Languages, or
building machine-learning models in R to classify animal behavior from accelerometer data for a
doctoral student in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology.[@dennisEtal2021] Ethics came along with
the methods. Phan and Ibraheem Ali, a sciences data librarian elsewhere in the
Library who also taught in the Carpentries program, organized cross-UC data ethics workshops for UC Love Data Week in 2021 and 2022 with colleagues at UC San Diego and UC
Berkeley, and published the model.[@phanEtal2021]

OCR is where the archive's old job met the new tools most directly. A great deal of research
evidence sits in scanned images no one can search or count: handwritten tables, printed
statistical series, text in scripts ordinary OCR software reads badly. In the unit's later years
Phan led DSC's work on getting computable text out of them, printed and handwritten alike,
and on transcribing recorded speech across languages. The projects came from researchers. For scanned Japanese documents about atomic-bomb survivors, the team compared six
tools to find one that could read dense historical Japanese. Handwritten nineteenth-century
German tables for a History professor, and handwritten German memoirs for a Sociology professor,
defeated standard OCR and needed a different route. The 1976 Iranian National Census sat locked
in scanned PDFs. A DataSquad student, Lukas Hager, built the core OCR pipeline those projects
shared, and other students containerized a layout-analysis workflow for medieval canon-law
texts. By 2026 the team had a triage tool that runs a fast baseline engine and a stronger AI
model side by side and recommends the cheapest defensible path to usable text for a given
collection.[^c-ocr] The same methods reached audio: transcribing interviews with dance scholars
for World Arts and Cultures, and processing recorded conversations for a dissertation in speech
research.

The team's approach to AI followed the archive's older instincts about stewardship. Where it
could, DSC ran open models on its own hardware, so sensitive research material did not leave
UCLA and researchers were not tied to a commercial service to read their own sources. AI and
machine learning also became a teaching line of its own, growing from a handful of sessions in
2023, and DSC staff published a Carpentries-style lesson on using AI coding agents in research
while keeping the work validated and reproducible.

Phan's later work carried the same habits into research software. After training at the
INTERSECT research-software-engineering bootcamp in 2025, she helped write a lesson on building
better research software, co-taught a UC Love Data Week 2026 workshop on making research
software citable and discoverable (doi:10.5281/zenodo.18615247), and became co-lead of UCLA's
open source program office.

[^c-ml-people]: Staffing per Dennis et al. 2021 [@dennisEtal2021] and the author's account.

[^c-ocr]: Project descriptions from DSC's own materials (the DataSquad project portfolio and a
2026 Powell Society presentation) and the `dsc-ocr-triage` repository (2026).

### DataSquad: a student research workforce

DataSquad borrowed its model from Carleton College, where a student-staffed data consulting
program had been given its own identity and structure.[@lackie2019] UCLA's version began in 2020
on a Norman Powell gift that paid the first cohort's salaries and laptops, and became a formal
program in 2021 under Tim; Leigh Phan became co-director in 2025. The Library added funds in 2023 to expand the
team and add in-person hours. In 2024 it absorbed the Lux Lab student line, and from 2025 a single
cohort of six was cross-trained to cover data consulting and 3D work alike.

Students worked with staff, not in front of them, and senior students ran project management.
Their share grew as staff capacity shrank. DataSquad students handled 190 of the unit's
scheduled consultations from 2023 to 2025, about a quarter, most of them in 2023. After that
their work moved toward sustained project support, where tracked tasks grew from 6 in 2023 to 111
in 2025, as departments started planning research around the team's availability rather than
calling only when something broke. Two long engagements show the kind of work. Lawrence Lee and
Madeline Kim rebuilt the pipeline for Carceral Ecologies' helicopter-surveillance data so that a
load that took about 318 minutes ran in about two. Julia Wood, Ethan Allavarpu, Tristan Dewing,
and Lee cleaned and restructured the BioCritical Studies Lab's national deaths-in-custody data,
cutting 41,466 records to 29,208 without losing what the lab needed, and built tools the lab
could maintain on its own.

It was also a pipeline. Of the ten students whose outcomes after graduation were tracked for
2023 to 2025, all went into data or technical roles, with McKinsey, Amazon, AIG, Stanford, and
CVS Health among the destinations; Julia Wood joined the Library as a data specialist. The model
has been picked up elsewhere through a DataSquad International network and written up in a
co-authored chapter in ACRL's *Data Culture*. Its research contributions are in the spotlights
under [Research impact](history.html#evidence-of-use).

### People and funding

Much of this era's expansion ran on Norman Powell's philanthropy: a data-scientist position, a
deep-learning machine and DSC space in the Young Research Library, infrastructure funds that
carried Dataverse's cloud costs for a time, and DataSquad's seed funding, all separate from his
dated $5M December 2016 gift that endowed the University Librarian position.

The people who carried the work were Jamie Jamison (repository and curation), Doug Daniels (3D
and emerging technology), Leigh Phan (programmer to data scientist, computational
research and AI), Zhiyuan Yao (spatial data science, until 2024), Kristian Allen (software
and machine learning, 2018–2024), a data-science facilitator, and the rotating DataSquad
students. The full roster, with what is and is not independently documented, is in
this companion.

Editorial questions that used to sit in the history's text as bracketed notes, moved here
2026-09-27, plus questions raised by the 2026-09-27 external reviews. Each affects only the detail
named; the history's public wording already reflects the uncertainty.

- Staffing: the Data Science Facilitator's name and dates; Leigh Phan's exact title and start
  date, and her titles before 2021; the 5-FTE peak year and the headcount at dissolution.
- Repository defense (2025 bot scraping): a ticket or postmortem reference to anchor the dates.
- Consultations: which figure, if any, to treat as the public number (1,175 service interactions
  2023–2025 vs. the 604 and 741 direct-consultation audits).
- Infrastructure funding: budget records for the infrastructure and dataset purchases funded from
  the freed subscription line; when campus consolidated the AWS accounts; when the Powell
  infrastructure funds ran out.
- Instruction: the validated DSC-wide instruction totals, once the instruction-stats integration
  is cleared for publication.

  past 2020.

  serves that data now.
- Text and machine learning: what the deep-learning workstation was used for; the text corpora
  bought with archive funds; when the OCR work started, whether the researchers can be named, and
  what each project produced.
- 3D student credit: which students did what on the "Boat of Hope." The Research Enabled by DSC claim
  register (§20) credits Daniels with the scan and Bianca Badajos with setting up the Potree
  viewer, and does not approve saying the student who processed the Iceland data joined the boat
  scan. `evidence/library-era-2014-present.md` (older) credits Badajos and Connor Lim with the
  scan; the register is newer and governs until the project record is checked. The public DataSquad
  portfolio page (`_portfolio/02-refugee-artifacts.md` on ucla-datasquad.github.io) also says the
  team was led by Daniels "with DataSquad members Bianca Badajos and Connor Lim," so three public
  accounts need to agree.
- DSC staff photo (2024, from the DataSquad site): captioned without names. Confirm who is
  pictured if names should be added.
- Iceland survey year: the companion's Daniels inventory has one trip in 2024 (per Tim
  2026-09-02); the claim register does not approve a year and notes the public pointcloud Iceland
  folder covers northern sites, not Mosfell Valley. Kept out of the main narrative until
  reconciled.
- Redivis processing volume: the history reads the 444 GB to 2.9 PB figures as platform-wide
  UCLA activity. Confirm the scope in the source (Tim's 2023–2025 Data Summary).
- Stale evidence note: `evidence/library-era-2014-present.md` still marks "DSC's work featured in
  Keel's book *The Coroner's Silence*" as verified; the claim register (2026-09-27) found no
  documented link, and the history no longer makes the claim. Update the evidence note.
- Dana Center grant: removed from the history's impact table 2026-09-27. The public announcement
  (UCLA and the Dana Foundation, April 2024) is a $5 million grant within a roughly $9.8 million

## Open discrepancies not yet resolved {#open-discrepancies}

- **1977 is not a founding.** Framing mostly settled. Tim, Stephenson's own Dataverse-page
  text, and Stiles & Stephenson 2008 all agree: the archive *function* ran continuously from the
  1960s (PBA, then the SRC's Archive Data Library, "reference-room basis only"); **1977 is when
  Treiman designed the research-support framework, the unit was named SSDA, and a Data Archivist
  line and consultative services were added.** The sources that "disagree" describe different
  facets: Stephenson credits Treiman and omits ISSR; the 2017 decks and the OECD directory name
  ISSR; the published book chapter [@dennisEtal2021] says "part of the Survey Research Center"
  (which by 1977 was a component of ISSR). **Still to check documentarily:** whether Treiman's
  1977 framework reported directly to ISSR or to SRC-within-ISSR. Confirm against the 1977–78
  UCLA General Catalog.
- **The 1964 SRC arrangement and Eve Fielder**: Stephenson's Dataverse-page text says the SRC
  formed in 1964 "under the direction of Eve Fielder" and the PBA merged into its planned Archive
  Data Library. A published obituary (LA Times, via legacy.com) says Fielder became SRC's *first*
  director only in **1976**, that SRC moved in **2004** to a Health Services Research division in
  UCLA General Internal Medicine, and that she was associate director there until retiring in
  **2006**. Either SRC ran from 1964 under someone else, or the account compresses two events.
  Not resolved against SRC's own records.
- **The ISSR-era director list and three-subperiod structure** (spot-verified 2026-09-02):
  **Sears's ISSR directorship 1993–2008** is independently confirmed (Wikipedia, UCLA psychology
  page). The three subperiods are grounded in the digitized UCLA General Catalogs
  (`evidence/deep-research-report.md` cites 2003–05 through 2013–14). Freeman's term (1974–1981)
  and Brewer's end (1993, when she left for Ohio State and Sears took over) are firm; **still
  open:** Brewer's start year, any gap 1981–1983, and whether the ISSR-to-ISR rename had a formal
  date/authority (none found).
- **ISSR-to-ISR rename and ISR dissolution**: no date or authority found for either; no director
  identified for the institute under the ISR name (~2009–2011).
- **The "8 founding members" of ICPSR, and "through his efforts"**: both phrasings are from
  Stephenson's Dataverse-page text, the archive's institutional memory, not an independent
  record. UCLA's founding-member status *is* primary-verified (Miller's 1962 memo). The "8" is
  not, Austin's list has 22, Miller's 21; "8" may be the "Committee of Eight" (1962–63
  correspondence in ICPSR's Bentley archive), unread. Marvick's personal founding role is
  undocumented (see the 1961–1964 section).
- **UC Carpentries workshop/learner counts**: Tim's SOPA states "28 workshops... 2,896 learners"
  for the 2023-2025 review period; his Data Summary states "37 workshops (2022–2025)... 1,495
  attendees (2024–2025)" for what may be a different scope (UC Carpentries alone vs. UCLA
  Carpentries + UC Carpentries combined) and a different date window. The founding/co-founding
  distinction (UCLA Carpentries 2018, UC Carpentries co-founded 2020) is resolved per Tim
  2026-08-09; the workshop counts are not. Use the SOPA's explicitly-scoped figure if one number
  is needed publicly.
- **Exact dates for three of Norman Powell's four gifts** (data scientist position, deep
  learning machine/DSC space, DataSquad seed funding), all undated in every source checked.
- **"The first reorg"**: Tim mentioned a first reorganization during the 2018-present span that
  reduced data-science support capacity. Recorded as a bare fact per the Method/independence
  note's discipline; not dated or elaborated, deliberately kept out of the public narrative
  entirely, not just trimmed, since this project's whole premise is staying independent of any
  reorg argument (see `history.qmd` Methods and limitations).
- **Jamie Jamison's DB dump / staff dates for 1977-1986**, tracked in
  `ucla-data-science-center/dataverse-infrastructure#10`, not yet received.
- **The Marvick Papers** (UCLA Special Collections, 63 boxes, 1955-1998), not yet consulted for
  primary founding documents, including Marvick's own 1967 proposal.
- **Tim's own 2021 book chapter**, "From a Data Archive to Data Science" (Dennis et al., in
  Herndon ed., *Data Science in the Library*, Facet, pp.99-109), not yet read; likely already
  contains a considered account of the 2014-2018 transition that predates and could sharpen
  everything reconstructed here piecemeal.

## Achievements resting only on performance-review language (not independently corroborated) {#review-only-claims}

Per the 2026-08-09 validate-external adjudication's evidence-tier rule (performance-review
documents are discovery sources, not sole public evidence): the following are real per Tim's or
Doug's self-authored review documents but have no independent corroboration found yet, and
should stay out of the public narrative until/unless corroborated:

- Leigh Phan's "deep learning work with Dennis" specifically (her independently-verified work is
  open-data/mapping and data-ethics instruction, real, but distinct from "deep learning").
- Zhiyuan Yao's GIS-analysis work specifically (independently verified: Carpentries workshop
  development; GIS-analysis project work itself not yet found under his name).
- The precise causal claim that Redivis/Carceral Ecologies/BioCritical Studies Lab outcomes
  constitute "impact" in the strongest sense (vs. documented activity/adoption/outcome), see
  `history.qmd` Research Impact for how this is handled with tiered language.

Full detail: `evidence/sopa-research-enabled-and-intellectual-contributions.md` and
`evidence/data-summaries-and-reconciliation.md`. Note: source documents for this section include
confidential peer-review letters, reference letters, and salary information not read for this
project and not summarized anywhere in this repository.
